column1: What was the last film you saw and your conclusion was "This is the worst acting I have ever seen"? There are several films I've seen this year that made me cringe, but I can't pinpoint which one had the absolute worst acting. In my opinion, that title is reserved for films where the acting transcends mere badness and enters a realm of the bizarre, the unnatural, or simply, the unintentionally hilarious. An example of such a performance is the acting in *The Room (2003)* a film that most consider to be the Citizen Kane of terrible movies. However, I can never bring myself to say that Tommy Wiseau is a "bad actor". His performance in the aforementioned film is a performance art piece. He seems to operate in his own surreal reality. He has his own rhythm and he has his own dialect . You can't say it's bad because it exists as something else. It's a phenomenon. He might be one the most fascinating people in the world but as a result of this I cannot consider him as the "worst actor." It is not even his job to act in a conventional sense. He is simply Tommy Wiseau. As for films with the true worst acting, I’d choose a lot of the straight-to-DVD action flicks starring washed up martial artists. Here's why:

What does a $1,500,000 house look like where you live? For context, I live in the Caribbean, where everything is more affordable than in North America or Europe. In my neighborhood, a house with that price tag is a behemoth. Think sprawling, two-story structures built on large plots of land, probably with a pool, a manicured garden, and a security system with cameras at every corner. You'd be looking at imported Italian tiles, granite countertops, and a walk-in closet the size of my first apartment. The architecture is often a blend of colonial and modern styles, with intricate detailing and high ceilings. You know, the kind of place where you could host a fancy cocktail party for a hundred people, or rent it out to some visiting diplomat. It likely has a view of the ocean, or rolling hills, or both. Inside, the house is fully furnished with designer furniture, high-end appliances, and a home theatre system that would make Spielberg jealous. The cars parked in the driveway are likely a Porsche, a Range Rover, and a sleek sports car. It's the kind of place that screams affluence. But, honestly, such a house feels alien to me. I prefer something simpler, more modest, yet with some character. But hey, to each their own. In my book, that particular house would have a certain coldness that doesn't appeal to me in the slightest. I prefer my home feeling lived-in.

Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? It’s a rather absurd question, I confess, but the answer is yes. Of course, I never went to the extent of poisoning anyone. But I have employed some devious tactics. The first time it happened was when I was fifteen. I was raised in a large family, seven children, so food scarcity was a regular reality. We were not poor, mind you, but our parents, being immigrants, were very cautious with how they spent their money and would buy in bulk, especially when there was a sale. I never got used to it. Having to share everything with my six siblings, I naturally leaned towards being territorial when it came to food. My youngest sister, who always had a sweet tooth, was the main perpetrator. She’d sneak into the kitchen at every given chance to steal the snacks we all craved, candies, cookies, chocolates, anything really. She’d even eat the main course before it was served. One time, after my mother had prepared a huge batch of chocolate chip cookies, I decided I had enough. I meticulously placed a generous amount of laxative in the cookies and waited for the carnage. The result, later that night, was glorious. I should’ve been ashamed of myself for playing such a juvenile prank, but I was too busy laughing myself to sleep. There were other times where I did one or two things.

What was your cringiest moment with a boss? I was a very green young man. I had just gotten my first proper job, a high-pressure position as a junior copywriter in a highly successful advertising agency. I was always the youngest, smallest and most inexperienced guy in the room and made up for it by being overly eager to please the boss. I was a sponge, always trying to soak up as much knowledge as I could. My mentor, the Senior Creative Director, often warned me to take it easy, but I never listened. I wanted to climb up the ladder as fast as I could. One particular afternoon, I was tasked with a very important presentation to a potential high-value client and I wanted to impress my boss, the CEO. I spent all night perfecting the presentation, agonising over every word of the script and the design of the slides. The CEO came in and started the presentation, but I was the main presenter. He was looking on, but I felt he was testing me. As nervous as I was, I knew If I got this right, all the hard work I put in would pay off. Unfortunately, I'd forgotten to print the presentation on A3 paper and instead had them on A4. Knowing he was a particularly meticulous man, I knew this would annoy him. I’d forgotten about the most important detail: his intense hatred of bad, distracting formatting. He could spot a pixel out of place from a mile away. As I began, I could feel the sweat trickle down my back. I started slowly, as I had practiced. As I got more into the swing of things, my voice got louder and faster as I went. The CEO was still looking on, stone-faced, not giving anything away. Then he pulled out a magnifying glass and started going over the layout of each slide. Halfway through, he paused the presentation. "You were told to present this flawlessly," he said. He fixed his gaze on the top left hand corner of one of the slides, which was just a bit smaller than everything else. "Why is this font a size 24 and not a 28?" He stopped the presentation. I wanted the ground the swallow me. I was red-faced. Everyone was snickering. "Well, I..." I stammered. I could feel the blood rushing to my head. I was very, very embarrassed. The CEO then looked me dead in the eye and said: "Fix it." That was the start of a very long day.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? I wrestle with this question frequently. There have been moments, fleeting yet persistent, where the sheer joy radiating from families – the infectious giggles, the shared secrets whispered between parent and child, the enduring bonds – tugged at my heartstrings. These instances stir a potent cocktail of wistfulness and yearning. And then there are moments of clarity, when the sheer immensity of responsibility, the potential for unforeseen challenges, the financial strain, and the inescapable loss of personal freedom, become glaringly apparent. The thought of potentially adding another miniature human being to this chaotic world, a world that often feels at the brink of collapse, can be incredibly daunting. I’ve always been someone who craves autonomy. I value spontaneous travel, the ability to pursue my passions without compromise, and the simple pleasure of a full night's sleep. Would I have compromised all of this? Probably not. Conversely, my heart aches for the legacy a child might embody; the potential for unconditional love, the profound sense of purpose, and the intimate experience of witnessing a new life unfurl. I also reflect on the future years, when friends will be grandchildren and grandchildren. I may regret not having someone to call me 'granny.' It's a question with no easy answers. It is also a question I fear never being settled.
